newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends firm but off highs vs yen, mark in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends firm but off highs vs yen, mark in Europe.

text.p: The dollar surrendered some of its early gains on profit-taking in late Europe after getting a leg-up on the mark and yen as Bill Clinton was returned to the White House and Republicans retained control of Congress.
"We have seen profit-taking across the board, especially on dollar/mark and dollar/yen," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
The dollar was cheered earlier as Clinton was returned to the presidency for a four-year term. There was also relief the Republicans retained control of Congress.
Dollar/mark ended the European session off highs at 1.5181/91 marks at 1524 GMT against 1.5140/47 late Tuesday.
Dollar/yen lost all of its shine on Wednesday to end at 113.88/3.98 against 113.90/4.00 late on Tuesday after rising briefly to session highs of 114.67 yen.
"It's a typical case of buy on the rumour and sell on the fact," added the trader.

With the U.S. election now behind, traders said the dollar will focus on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on November 13. "The focus remains on the Fed...Though the FOMC next week is not expected to raise interest rates, there is still the focus on U.S. growth and interest rates," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank.
U.S. analysts on Wednesday said Clinton will likely maintain a hands-off stance towards the country's central bank, which they say has paid great dividends.
But some are wary of the dollar's strength.

With Wall Street still in the stratosphere and bond markets firm it can be argued that both are overdue for a shakeout. If there is to be a fall in asset markets, best get it out of the way early on in the administration, analysts said.
"The big risk is a policy change," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International. "But a policy change would be initiated only by the U.S., not the Japanese or the Germans."
Longer-term, Standard Chartered's Fox said changes in the G3 economic balance will be driving currency markets in the next year as both German and Japanese growth strengthens.
"U.S. growth will remain steady to firm, but it is not necessarily getting much better and therefore narrowing in its growth differentials between Germany and Japan," Fox added.

A late bout of weakness in the dollar against the German mark was partly attributed to talk a major German bank had raised the possibility of a delay to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) with its customers. At 1605 GMT dollar/mark was at 1.5164/70.
The mark ended steady to slighty firmer on its European crosses in late Europe, after reversing early losses made following the U.S. election results.
Despite minor day-to-day jitters the market seems to be sounding out the reference rates at which monetary union will be irrevocably fix exchange rates.

The European Commission released its semi-annual economic report and said EU growth will pick up next year. It said all but Italy, the U.K, and Greece would next year meet the buget deficit criteria necessary to start EMU in 1999.
